newsitem.title: FRANCE: German, French officials seek to keep lid on dollar.
newsitem.headline: German, French officials seek to keep lid on dollar.

text.p: German and French monetary officials on Wednesday engaged in another bout of verbal intervention in the currency markets in a bid to stem the dollar's rise against the mark, saying the U.S. currency had risen far enough.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, reflecting Bundesbank concern that the mark's recent depreciation may boost inflation in Germany, reiterated that the mark's sharp rise in 1995 had now been fully corrected and said the Bundesbank was not interested in a further weakening of the mark.

Tietmeyer said currency markets had clearly understood a statement released after a meeting of finance leaders of the Group of Seven leading industrialised countries last month in Berlin, which said the dollar's correction has been completed.
"We do not want to see a correction that goes beyond the market fundamentals," Tietmeyer told a news conference following a Franco-German economic summit meeting here.
"We are interested in a stable mark, we assume France is interested in a stable franc and we are both interested in a stable euro."
His view was echoed by French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis who told the news conference that current exchange rate levels should be consolidated.
The comments weakened the dollar by about a third of a pfenning. By 1455 GMT it traded at 1.7034/39.
Earlier, Arthuis said in a newspaper interview published on Wednesday that he was pleased by the dollar's rise against Europe's currencies which he called a fair appreciation.
"At each G7 meeting we regretted this weakening of the dollar," Arthuis said. "So let's not spoil our pleasure."
He added that the dollar's rise reflected not a change in the German economy but a fair appreciation of the dollar.

The mark's steep depreciation against the dollar and other European currencies like the British pound and the Italian lira in recent months has helped boost German exports by making German products cheaper abroad.

While the latest economic data showed that German economic output stagnated in the final quarter of 1996, most analysts forecast a pick-up in the course of the year, helped by rising exports, low interest rates and an expected rise in domestic investment as capacity utilisation increases.
But the mark's fall has also fuelled import prices and Bundesbank officials have warned that if the depreciation goes on Germany runs the risk of importing inflation.
Import prices climbed 2.6 percent in January from a year ago, the strongest rise since May 1991 in what the Federal Statistics Office attributed to the stronger dollar and higher oil prices.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said last week that the he saw no danger at present of German price pressures rising but added that the mark must not fall further because this could fuel inflation.
Although the Bundesbank can do much to control the level of domestic price growth, it has historically faced difficulty in protecting Germany from price developments abroad.

Economists however remain confident that for the moment, consumer inflation is likely to remain tame and that the Bundesbank will have no need to raise interest rates until later this year or in 1998.
In February, preliminary west German inflation was 0.4 percent month-on-month and 1.8 percent year-on-year, a slight decline from January's respective rates of 0.5 percent and 1.9 percent.
